why_how.text: The tests draw on specific sections of the manual, so knowing them focuses your study.
Sample questions help you review, but they are not the whole test.
Each practice test topic maps to specific chapters, and Rules of the Road spans four of them.

scenario.text: Ava plans to study only the sample questions at the end of each chapter.

reasoning.text: The sample questions come from the test, but the test can draw on many other questions, so they are a review aid rather than the full question set.

result.text: Ava studies Sections B and C and uses the sample questions only to review.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking the chapter sample questions are the whole test.

correction.text: The sample questions are a review aid; the test can draw on many other questions from Sections B and C.

memory_support.text: Study B and C; samples review, practice teaches.

prompt.text: Which practice test topic covers four chapters of the manual?

rationale.text: Traffic Signs and Signals and Alcohol, Other Drugs and Driving each map to a single chapter.

lines.text: Sections B and C are the material.
Sample questions help you review.

narration.text: Sections B and C of the manual are the study material for both the learner permit test and the driver license test. This short lesson explains how to use the manual well. You will see how the sample questions fit in, why the manual alone cannot make you a driver, and how the online practice tests line up with the chapters. Knowing where the test material comes from lets you spend your study time on the right pages, and knowing how practice tests are grouped lets you check each topic on its own before test day. Remember: The manual by itself cannot teach you to drive; driving skill comes from a good instructor and lots of practice.

lines.text: They come from the test.
The test has many other questions too.
Use them as a review aid.

narration.text: The sample questions at the end of each chapter come from the test, but the test can draw on many other questions, so they are a review aid rather than the full question set. That means memorizing the sample answers is not enough. Read the chapters in Sections B and C, then use the sample questions to check what you remember. If you miss a sample question, go back to the chapter and reread the topic, because the test may ask about the same idea in a different way than the sample does. Remember: Sections B and C of the manual are the study material for both the learner permit test and the driver license test.

lines.text: Grouped by topic.
Guidelines for Driving matches the first two Section B chapters.

narration.text: The online practice tests are grouped by topic, and the Guidelines for Driving practice test matches the first two chapters of Section B. The Rules of the Road practice test spans four chapters of Section B, while Traffic Signs and Signals maps to a single chapter and Alcohol, Other Drugs and Driving maps to a single chapter. So when a practice test on one topic goes badly, you know exactly which chapters to reread. Rules of the Road needs the most reading, since it covers four chapters rather than one. Remember: The manual by itself cannot teach you to drive; driving skill comes from a good instructor and lots of practice.

lines.text: Reading does not build driving skill.
A good instructor and practice do.

narration.text: Here is a common misunderstanding. Some new drivers believe that knowing the manual well means they know how to drive. The manual by itself cannot teach you to drive; driving skill comes from a good instructor and lots of practice. The manual gives you the rules and the knowledge the tests check, but handling a car comes only from time behind the wheel with good guidance. Use the manual to learn what to do, and use practice with an instructor to learn how to do it smoothly and safely on real roads. Remember: Sections B and C of the manual are the study material for both the learner permit test and the driver license test.

lines.text: Which topic spans four chapters?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: you want to review the practice test topic that covers the most chapters of Section B. Which topic is it? Work it out before reading on. It is Rules of the Road, which spans four chapters. Traffic Signs and Signals maps to just one chapter, and so does Alcohol, Other Drugs and Driving. The Guidelines for Driving practice test matches the first two chapters of Section B. Because Rules of the Road spreads across the most chapters, it is the topic that will need the most reading time. Remember: The online practice tests are grouped by topic, and the Guidelines for Driving practice test matches Chapters B-one and B-two of the manual.

lines.text: Read Sections B and C.
Review with samples and practice tests.
Build skill with an instructor.

narration.text: To wrap up, Sections B and C are the study material for both the learner permit and the driver license tests. The chapter sample questions come from the test but are only a review aid, because the test can draw on many other questions. The online practice tests are grouped by topic, with Rules of the Road spanning four chapters and the other topics mapping more narrowly. Finally, the manual alone cannot teach you to drive; that skill comes from a good instructor and lots of practice behind the wheel. Remember: The manual by itself cannot teach you to drive; driving skill comes from a good instructor and lots of practice.

why_how.text: Checks before you start prevent hazards around and inside the car.
A correct seat position protects you in a crash and keeps you in control.

scenario.text: Raj likes to drive with his seat leaned back and sitting close to the steering wheel.

reasoning.text: A reclined seat cuts your view and slows your reaction, and your body should be roughly ten to twelve inches from the wheel so an air bag strikes your chest.

result.text: Raj sits upright and moves back to about ten to twelve inches from the wheel.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking the head restraint is just a comfortable headrest.

correction.text: The head restraint is there to prevent whiplash when you are struck from behind, so raise it level with the back of your head.

memory_support.text: Walk around, learn controls, sit up, ten to twelve back.

prompt.text: How far from the steering wheel should your body be, and why?

answer.text: Roughly ten to twelve inches, so a deploying air bag strikes your chest instead of your chin or face.

rationale.text: The distance applies whether or not the car has an air bag.

lines.text: Check outside the car.
Learn the controls.
Set your seat.

narration.text: Safe driving starts before the engine does. Before getting in, walk around the vehicle and look for small children, pets or anything else in the way. The outside check also covers the windows, lights, body damage, tire condition and any sign of fluid leaking. This lesson takes you from that walk-around to the driver's seat, where you will learn the controls and set the seat, steering wheel and head restraint so that you can see well, reach everything easily and stay protected if a crash happens. Remember: The top of the steering wheel should sit no higher than the tops of your shoulders.

lines.text: Key in, doors locked.
Find every switch, gauge and pedal.
Know them before you need them.

narration.text: After getting in, put the key in the ignition, lock the doors and learn where every switch, gauge and pedal is and what it does. You should know where the horn, turn signals, four-way flashers, headlight and dimmer switch, wiper and washer controls, parking brake and release, climate and defroster controls and gearshift are even before you need them. The point is to find them without searching. In a sudden rainstorm or an emergency, there is no time to hunt for the wiper switch or the flashers. Remember: The top of the steering wheel should sit no higher than the tops of your shoulders.

lines.text: Never reclined.
Heel on the floor, foot glides between pedals.
Clear view of windows and mirrors.

narration.text: Never drive with the seat reclined or partly reclined, because it cuts your view and slows your reaction in an emergency. Set the seat so the pedals are easy to reach and your foot can glide from the accelerator to the brake while your heel stays on the floor. Do not slide the seat so far forward, or pull the steering column out so far, that steering becomes awkward. Your seat position should give a clear view through the windshield, both side windows and every mirror. Remember: The top of the steering wheel should sit no higher than the tops of your shoulders.

lines.text: Ten to twelve inches from the wheel.
Wheel top no higher than your shoulders.

narration.text: Keep your body roughly ten to twelve inches from the steering wheel, whether or not the car has an air bag, so a deploying air bag strikes your chest instead of your chin or face. The top of the steering wheel should sit no higher than the tops of your shoulders. These two settings work together. Sitting at the right distance with the wheel at the right height keeps your face out of the air bag's path and gives you full control of the wheel, without reaching or crowding it. Remember: Your seat position should give a clear view through the windshield, both side windows and every mirror.

lines.text: Not just a headrest.
Raise it level with the back of your head.
Prevents whiplash from behind.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Many drivers think the head restraint is simply a place to rest your head, and they leave it wherever it happens to be. The head restraint is there to prevent whiplash when you are struck from behind. Raise it until it is level with the back of your head. A restraint set too low does not support your head in a rear impact. Check it every time you adjust the seat, and remember that the seat must not be reclined either, since reclining cuts your view and slows your reaction. Remember: Never drive with the seat reclined or partly reclined, because it cuts your view and slows your reaction in an emergency.

lines.text: How far from the wheel, and why?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: how far from the steering wheel should your body be, and what is the reason? Work it out before reading on. Keep your body roughly ten to twelve inches from the steering wheel, whether or not the car has an air bag. At that distance, a deploying air bag strikes your chest instead of your chin or face. Pair that with a steering wheel whose top sits no higher than your shoulders and a seat that lets your foot glide between the pedals with your heel on the floor. Remember: The top of the steering wheel should sit no higher than the tops of your shoulders.

lines.text: Walk around and check the car.
Learn every control.
Seat upright, wheel distance, head restraint.

narration.text: To close, walk around the car to look for children, pets and obstacles and to check the windows, lights, body, tires and any leaks. Inside, put the key in, lock the doors and learn every control before you need it. Never drive reclined, set the seat so your foot glides between pedals with your heel down, keep a clear view of all windows and mirrors, sit ten to twelve inches from the wheel with its top no higher than your shoulders, and raise the head restraint to the back of your head. Remember: The top of the steering wheel should sit no higher than the tops of your shoulders.

why_how.text: Well-set mirrors give the widest view with the smallest blind spots.
No mirror setting removes every blind spot.
Each outside mirror is set from its own head position until your car barely shows.

scenario.text: Lena sets her left mirror so that half of it shows the side of her own car.

reasoning.text: The left mirror should be set, with your head against the driver's window, until the side of your car just barely shows at its inner edge.

result.text: Lena turns the mirror outward until only a sliver of her car shows.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking well-adjusted mirrors remove all blind spots.

correction.text: Even perfectly adjusted mirrors leave some blind spots, so always turn your head to check before turning or changing lanes.

memory_support.text: Seat first, mirrors next, head check always.

prompt.text: You are about to adjust the passenger-side outside mirror. Where should your head be while you set it, and what should the mirror show?

answer.text: Hold your head just above the center console and set it until the side of your car just barely shows at its inner edge.

rationale.text: The left mirror uses the same idea, but with your head against the driver's window.

lines.text: Seat first, then mirrors.
Widest view, smallest blind spots.

narration.text: Your car has three rearview mirrors: the inside mirror and two outside mirrors. Adjust all three only after the seat is set, and always before you start driving, aiming for the widest view and the smallest blind spots. This lesson shows how to set each mirror, how to check the settings with a passing car, and what to do when a mirror still shows too much of your own car. It ends with the most important point of all: even perfect mirrors leave blind spots, so your head still has a job to do. Remember: Adjust all three rearview mirrors only after the seat is set, and always before you start driving, aiming for the widest view and the smallest blind spots.

lines.text: Frame the rear window.
Only the edge of the right rear post shows.

narration.text: Set the inside mirror to frame the rear window, turned so that only the edge of the right rear window post shows. That gives you a full view straight behind the car. Because the outside mirrors are set from the seated position too, the inside mirror and the outside mirrors should work as a team, with each one covering a different part of the area behind and beside you. Set the inside mirror first, then move on to the left and right outside mirrors, which each use a simple head-position trick to get the angle right. Remember: Adjust all three rearview mirrors only after the seat is set, and always before you start driving, aiming for the widest view and the smallest blind spots.

lines.text: Left: head against the driver's window.
Right: head just above the center console.
Your car barely shows at the inner edge.

narration.text: For the left mirror, rest your head against the driver's window and set the mirror until the side of your car just barely shows at its inner edge. For the right mirror, hold your head just above the center console and set it until the side of your car just barely shows at its inner edge. A car without remote mirror controls may need a helper to set the passenger-side mirror correctly. In both cases, the aim is to see only a sliver of your own car, leaving the rest of the mirror for the lanes beside you. Remember: Set the inside mirror to frame the rear window, turned so that only the edge of the right rear window post shows.

lines.text: Let a car pass on your left.
Bumper appears as it leaves the inside mirror.
Try new settings while parked.

narration.text: To check the mirrors, let a car pass on your left: as it leaves the inside mirror, its front bumper should appear in the left outside mirror. If leaning back a little still shows you more than a glimpse of your car's rear corners in the outside mirrors, turn those mirrors outward. Try new mirror settings while parked, for example along a street watching passing cars, before driving into traffic with them. That way you learn the new view safely before you depend on it at speed. Remember: A car without remote mirror controls may need a helper to set the passenger-side mirror correctly.

lines.text: No setting removes every blind spot.
Turn your head before turning or changing lanes.

narration.text: Here is the trap. After setting all three mirrors carefully, many drivers believe they can see everything around the car. They cannot. Even perfectly adjusted mirrors leave some blind spots, so always turn your head to check before turning or changing lanes. The mirrors shrink the blind spots, but they never erase them. A quick look over your shoulder covers the area the mirrors miss. Make that head check a habit every time, because a car hidden in a blind spot is invisible in every mirror you have. Remember: Adjust all three rearview mirrors only after the seat is set, and always before you start driving, aiming for the widest view and the smallest blind spots.

lines.text: Where is your head when setting the right mirror?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: you are setting the right outside mirror. Where should your head be, and what should the mirror show? Work it out before reading on. Hold your head just above the center console and set the mirror until the side of your car just barely shows at its inner edge. The left mirror uses the same idea, but with your head resting against the driver's window. If a car without remote mirror controls makes the right mirror hard to set, a helper can adjust it while you sit in the driver's seat. Remember: A car without remote mirror controls may need a helper to set the passenger-side mirror correctly.

lines.text: Inside mirror frames the rear window.
Outside mirrors show a sliver of your car.
Always check over your shoulder.

narration.text: To wrap up, set the seat first and the mirrors before every drive. Frame the rear window in the inside mirror, and set each outside mirror from its own head position until your car barely shows at the inner edge. Check the handoff with a passing car, turn the mirrors outward if you see more than a glimpse of your rear corners, and try new settings while parked. Most important, even perfect mirrors leave blind spots, so always turn your head to check before turning or changing lanes. Remember: Set the inside mirror to frame the rear window, turned so that only the edge of the right rear window post shows.

why_how.text: Buckling up and starting correctly come before every trip.
Knowing your transmission tells you which gear to use and which habits are illegal.
A manual transmission uses the clutch at set moments: starting, shifting and stopping.

scenario.text: Nico is starting a manual car for the first time.

reasoning.text: A manual car needs the parking brake set and the clutch pressed before it will start, and it should be in NEUTRAL with your foot on the brake.

result.text: Nico sets the parking brake, presses the clutch and the brake, and starts the car in NEUTRAL.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking it is fine to coast downhill with the gears in neutral.

correction.text: Coasting with the gears in neutral is illegal, and you should not rest your foot on the clutch when you are not changing gears.

memory_support.text: Buckle up, brake down, check the lights, never coast.

prompt.text: When must you push the clutch all the way down in a manual car?

answer.text: When starting, when shifting and once your speed falls below ten miles per hour while stopping.

rationale.text: At other times keep your foot off the clutch, and never coast in neutral.

lines.text: Belts before driving.
Starting the engine.
Using the transmission.

narration.text: This lesson covers the first steps of every drive: buckling up, starting the engine and using the transmission. Wear the lap belt snug across your hips and the shoulder belt snug across your shoulder, and make sure every passenger is belted or in a child restraint before you drive. Failing to belt yourself or to secure passengers in a car seat or booster seat can bring a fine. With everyone secure, you are ready to start the engine, check the dashboard and choose the right gear for the drive ahead. Remember: Coasting with the gears in neutral is illegal, and you should not rest your foot on the clutch when you are not changing gears.

lines.text: Foot on the brake.
Automatic in PARK, manual in NEUTRAL.
Manual: parking brake set, clutch pressed.

narration.text: To start most cars, keep your foot on the brake with an automatic in PARK or a manual in NEUTRAL. A manual car needs the parking brake set and the clutch pressed before it will start. With the key turned to on, check the dashboard lights and gauges, such as the antilock brake, air bag and fuel indicators, for warnings. Use low-beam headlights especially at night or in bad weather; even in normal daylight, headlights make a vehicle visible from twice as far away. Then you are ready to choose a gear. Remember: Coasting with the gears in neutral is illegal, and you should not rest your foot on the clutch when you are not changing gears.

lines.text: R is reverse, D is drive.
O is overdrive for interstates.
L, two or one for special cases.

narration.text: In an automatic car, R is reverse and D is drive, and some newer cars add an O overdrive setting meant for interstates with little stop-and-go traffic. The lower gears marked L, two or one are for special cases such as steep mountain descents, slow driving on ice or slippery roads, and slowing down if the brakes fail. So in ordinary driving you use drive, on open interstates you may use overdrive, and you save the low gears for steep hills, slippery roads or a brake failure. Remember: Coasting with the gears in neutral is illegal, and you should not rest your foot on the clutch when you are not changing gears.

lines.text: Clutch down to start, shift and stop.
Downshift on steep hills.

narration.text: With a manual transmission, push the clutch all the way down when starting, when shifting and once your speed falls below ten miles per hour while stopping. A manual transmission lets the driver use gears instead of brakes to help slow the car, and you should shift to a lower gear going down steep hills. So the clutch is pressed only for specific moments, and the gears themselves can help control your speed on a long downhill, easing the work your brakes must do on the way down. Remember: Coasting with the gears in neutral is illegal, and you should not rest your foot on the clutch when you are not changing gears.

lines.text: Coasting in neutral is illegal.
Do not rest your foot on the clutch.
Never turn the ignition to lock while moving.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Some drivers think coasting downhill in neutral saves effort. Coasting with the gears in neutral is illegal, and you should not rest your foot on the clutch when you are not changing gears. Another danger involves the ignition. In a car with a steering wheel interlock, never turn the ignition to lock while moving, because the wheel will lock and you will lose control. Keep the car in gear, keep your foot off the clutch between shifts, and leave the ignition alone until you have stopped. Remember: With the key turned to on, check the dashboard lights and gauges, such as the antilock brake, air bag and fuel indicators, for warnings.

lines.text: When does the clutch go all the way down?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: in a manual car, when must you push the clutch all the way down? Work it out before reading on. Push it all the way down when starting, when shifting, and once your speed falls below ten miles per hour while stopping. At other times, keep your foot off the clutch, because resting your foot on it when you are not changing gears is a habit to avoid. And never take the car out of gear to coast, because coasting with the gears in neutral is illegal. Remember: Coasting with the gears in neutral is illegal, and you should not rest your foot on the clutch when you are not changing gears.

lines.text: Everyone belted.
Brake down to start; check the dash.
Right gear, no coasting.

narration.text: To close, buckle the lap and shoulder belts snugly and secure every passenger, since unbelted occupants can bring a fine. Start with your foot on the brake, an automatic in PARK or a manual in NEUTRAL with the parking brake set and clutch pressed, then check the dashboard warnings and use low beams. Use drive or overdrive normally and low gears for special cases, press the clutch only to start, shift and stop, downshift on steep hills, never coast in neutral, and never turn the ignition to lock while moving. Remember: Coasting with the gears in neutral is illegal, and you should not rest your foot on the clutch when you are not changing gears.

why_how.text: Good hand position keeps you in control and reduces air bag injuries.
Push-pull and hand-over-hand steering trade speed for control.

scenario.text: Sofia turns left using push-pull steering for the first time.

reasoning.text: In a push-pull left turn, the left hand pulls down to about seven o'clock while the right hand pushes up to about one o'clock.

result.text: Sofia keeps both hands on the wheel the whole turn, then reverses the movements to straighten out.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking crossing your arms during a turn is the same as crossing your wrists.

correction.text: Crossing your wrists during a turn is fine, but crossing your arms is not, because clothing or jewelry can snag and an air bag would injure you more.

memory_support.text: Nine and three, push-pull, reverse to return.

prompt.text: Why is push-pull the recommended way to steer?

answer.text: It slows the turn and keeps both hands on the wheel the whole time.

rationale.text: Hand-over-hand is faster but can leave only one hand on the wheel.

lines.text: A relaxed, firm grip with both hands.
Steer with your eyes too.

narration.text: This lesson covers how to hold the steering wheel and how to turn it. Keep both hands on the wheel with a relaxed but firm grip, and do not prop your elbow on the door or hang your arm out the window. You also steer with your eyes as well as your hands: look where you want to go, and let your side vision help hold your lane position. From there we move to exact hand positions and the two steering methods the manual describes, push-pull and hand-over-hand, and how each one affects your control. Remember: You steer with your eyes as well as your hands: look where you want to go, and let your side vision help hold your lane position.

lines.text: Left hand at nine, right at three.
Helps avoid air bag injuries.
Elbows slightly bent.

narration.text: Picture the wheel as a clock and put your left hand at nine o'clock and your right at three o'clock, a position that helps avoid air bag injuries. Your elbows should bend slightly when your palm reaches the top of the wheel, and you should never sit with your arms locked straight. Your hand position will change briefly while you work the turn signal, headlight dimmer or wiper controls, but you return to nine and three as soon as you are done. This is your home position for normal driving. Remember: An arm resting on the door or out the window gives you less control of the wheel and could be severed in a sideswipe.

lines.text: No elbow on the door.
No arm out the window.

narration.text: An arm resting on the door or out the window gives you less control of the wheel and could be severed in a sideswipe. That is why the manual tells you not to prop your elbow on the door or hang your arm out the window. Both hands belong on the wheel with a relaxed but firm grip. A driver with one arm out the window has only one hand ready for a sudden swerve, and that arm is exposed if another vehicle passes too close. Keep both arms inside the car and both hands on the wheel. Remember: Keep both hands on the wheel with a relaxed but firm grip, and do not prop your elbow on the door or hang your arm out the window.

lines.text: Recommended method.
Slows the turn, keeps both hands on.
Left turn: pull to seven, push to one.

narration.text: The push-pull method is the recommended way to steer because it slows the turn and keeps both hands on the wheel the whole time. In a push-pull left turn, the left hand pulls down to about seven o'clock while the right pushes up to about one o'clock. A right turn mirrors this, with the right hand pulling to about five o'clock and the left pushing to about eleven. Coming out of a turn, reverse the hand movements instead of letting the wheel slide through your fingers. Remember: In a push-pull left turn the left hand pulls down to about seven o'clock while the right pushes up to about one o'clock; a right turn mirrors this, with the right hand pulling to about five and the left pushing to about eleven.

lines.text: Faster, but hands cross at the top.
Sometimes only one hand on the wheel.
Keep speed down.

narration.text: Hand-over-hand steering turns the wheel faster but crosses the hands at the top and sometimes leaves only one hand on the wheel, so keep your speed down when using it. For a hand-over-hand right turn, reach forward to grip the rim at one o'clock palm down, pull to five o'clock, repeat with the other hand, and return to nine and three before counter-steering out. Counter-steering, reversing the hand movements out of a turn, also helps in skids and on snow and ice. Remember: Coming out of a turn, reverse the hand movements instead of letting the wheel slide through your fingers; this counter-steering also helps in skids and on snow and ice.

lines.text: Crossing wrists: fine.
Crossing arms: not fine.

narration.text: Here is a detail that trips people up. Crossing your wrists during a turn is fine, but crossing your arms is not, because clothing or jewelry can snag and an air bag would injure you more. The difference matters most in hand-over-hand turns, where the hands cross at the top of the wheel. Keep the crossing at the wrists. If your forearms end up crossed over each other, you have turned too far with one hand, and you are in the position the manual warns against. Push-pull avoids the problem entirely. Remember: Hand-over-hand steering turns the wheel faster but crosses the hands at the top and sometimes leaves only one hand on the wheel, so keep your speed down when using it.

lines.text: Why is push-pull recommended?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: the manual describes two steering methods. Why is push-pull the recommended one? Work it out before reading on. Push-pull slows the turn and keeps both hands on the wheel the whole time. Hand-over-hand turns the wheel faster, but it crosses the hands at the top and sometimes leaves only one hand on the wheel, which is why you keep your speed down when using it. With either method, you finish a turn by reversing the hand movements rather than letting the wheel slide. Remember: The push-pull method is the recommended way to steer because it slows the turn and keeps both hands on the wheel the whole time.

lines.text: Both hands, nine and three.
Push-pull is recommended.
Reverse the hands to return.

narration.text: To wrap up, hold the wheel with both hands at nine and three, with a relaxed but firm grip and elbows slightly bent, and keep your arms inside the car. Steer with your eyes by looking where you want to go. Push-pull steering, pulling to seven and pushing to one for a left turn, is recommended because both hands stay on the wheel. Hand-over-hand is faster but needs lower speed. Cross your wrists if needed but never your arms, and reverse your hands coming out of every turn. Remember: An arm resting on the door or out the window gives you less control of the wheel and could be severed in a sideswipe.

why_how.text: Backing is where new drivers make predictable mistakes.
Rear-end crashes are Tennessee's most common type, so smooth stops matter.

scenario.text: Mateo is about to back out of his driveway.

reasoning.text: To back up, hold the wheel at twelve o'clock with your left hand, put your right arm over the seat back and look through the rear window, keeping to idle speed or gentle acceleration.

result.text: Mateo turns, looks out the rear window and backs slowly until the car has fully stopped.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking you should stop past the stop line if there is no crosswalk.

correction.text: Stop before the crosswalk or marked stop line; if there is neither, stop where you can see traffic on the cross road before entering the intersection.

memory_support.text: Back slow and look back; stop smooth and before the line.

prompt.text: Where do you stop at a stop sign with no crosswalk and no stop line?

answer.text: Where you can see traffic on the cross road, before entering the intersection.

rationale.text: With a crosswalk or stop line, you stop before it.

lines.text: Backing up.
Pulling away.
Stopping and parking.

narration.text: This lesson covers the basic moves: backing up, pulling away, stopping and parking at a curb. New drivers backing up most often go too fast, steer too much or turn the wheel the wrong way. Those three errors give you a checklist to avoid. When pulling away, look at least one block ahead and steer toward a reference point. And because Tennessee reports rear-end collisions as the most common type of crash each year, smooth, planned stops matter on every trip. Each move has a simple routine you can practice until it becomes automatic.

lines.text: Left hand at twelve o'clock.
Right arm over the seat, look out the rear window.
Idle speed, look back until stopped.

narration.text: To back up, hold the wheel at twelve o'clock with your left hand, put your right arm over the seat back and look through the rear window, turning the wheel toward the side you want to move to. While backing, keep to idle speed or gentle acceleration and keep looking to the rear until the car has fully stopped. This routine answers each common error: idle speed prevents going too fast, small steering inputs prevent steering too much, and turning the wheel toward where you want to go keeps you from turning it the wrong way. Remember: New drivers backing up most often go too fast, steer too much or turn the wheel the wrong way.

lines.text: Check ahead, sides and behind.
Signal if leaving a curb.
Press the accelerator gently.

narration.text: Before pulling forward, check ahead, to the sides and behind, signal if leaving a curb, then move your foot to the accelerator and press gently. As you move off, look at least one block ahead and steer toward a reference point. Looking well ahead helps you drive straight and gives you time to see what is coming. Once you become a competent driver, the safest habit is not letting your attention to driving slip. The routine of checking, signaling and easing on the gas should stay the same however experienced you become. Remember: When pulling away, look at least one block ahead and steer toward a reference point.

lines.text: Check mirrors.
Ease off the accelerator.
Steady pressure on the brake.

narration.text: Tennessee reports rear-end collisions as the most common type of crash each year, which is why smooth, planned stops matter. For a smooth stop, check your mirrors, ease off the accelerator, move your foot to the brake and press with steady pressure rather than stomping. Checking the mirrors first tells you whether a driver behind you is close, and easing off and braking steadily gives that driver time to slow down too. A sudden, stomping stop is exactly the kind that invites a rear-end collision from the car behind. Remember: When parking at a curb, pull within eighteen inches of it.

lines.text: Before the crosswalk or stop line.
No markings: where you can see cross traffic.
Never inside the intersection.

narration.text: Here is the trap. When an intersection has no crosswalk and no stop line, some drivers roll forward and stop wherever they like. At a stop sign or signal, stop before the crosswalk or marked stop line. If there is neither, stop where you can see traffic on the cross road before entering the intersection. So the stopping point is always before the intersection, either at the marking or at the point where you can see cross traffic. Stopping inside the intersection is never the answer. Remember: When parking at a curb, pull within eighteen inches of it.

lines.text: No crosswalk or line: where do you stop?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: you approach a stop sign at an intersection with no crosswalk and no marked stop line. Where should you stop? Work it out before reading on. Stop where you can see traffic on the cross road, before entering the intersection. If there had been a crosswalk or a marked stop line, you would stop before it. Either way, make the stop smooth: check your mirrors, ease off the accelerator and press the brake with steady pressure, because rear-end collisions are Tennessee's most common type of crash. Remember: Tennessee reports rear-end collisions as the most common type of crash each year, which is why smooth, planned stops matter.

lines.text: Back slowly, looking back.
Look a block ahead pulling away.
Smooth stops; park within eighteen inches.

narration.text: To close, back up with your left hand at twelve o'clock, your right arm over the seat and your eyes on the rear window, at idle speed, turning toward where you want to go. Before pulling forward, check all around, signal from a curb and press gently, looking a block ahead. Stop smoothly with steady brake pressure, before the crosswalk or stop line or where you can see cross traffic. When parking at a curb, pull within eighteen inches of it, and never let your attention slip. Remember: When pulling away, look at least one block ahead and steer toward a reference point.

why_how.text: Carbon monoxide is a hidden danger you cannot sense.
Tennessee's hands-free law sets strict limits on phone use while driving.

scenario.text: Jade, seventeen, drives through a marked school zone with its flashers on and wants to take a call in hands-free mode.

reasoning.text: Drivers eighteen or older may use hands-free mode there, but the hands-free exception does not cover drivers under eighteen, for whom hand-held use is a delinquent act.

result.text: Jade does not use her phone in the school zone.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking the phone law only bans texting.

correction.text: The hands-free law bans holding a phone or device with any part of the body, as well as writing, sending or reading text messages.

memory_support.text: Hands off the phone; never run the engine closed in.

prompt.text: What does the Hands Free Tennessee law forbid a driver to do with a phone?

answer.text: Hold it with any part of the body, or write, send or read any text-based message.

rationale.text: The law also forbids reaching out of your belted position for a device or using video on it.

lines.text: Carbon monoxide.
Phones and screens.

narration.text: This lesson covers two dangers that are easy to overlook: carbon monoxide and distraction from phones and screens. Carbon monoxide from the engine can kill, and it cannot be tasted, smelled or seen. It tends to leak while the heater runs, when the exhaust system is faulty, or from other cars' fumes in heavy traffic. Then we turn to Tennessee's phone laws, including the Hands Free Tennessee law, the special rules in marked school zones, and where video screens may and may not be installed in a car. Remember: Under the Hands Free Tennessee law, a driver may not hold a phone or mobile device with any part of the body or write, send or read any text-based message.

lines.text: Never run the engine in a closed garage.
No heater or air in a closed parked car.
Check the exhaust, close the vent in traffic.

narration.text: Never run the engine in a closed garage, and never use the heater or air conditioner in a parked car with the windows shut. To guard against carbon monoxide, have the exhaust checked regularly, listen for unusual roaring under the car and close the fresh-air vent in heavy traffic. Each step targets one of the ways the gas gets in: a closed space traps it, a faulty exhaust leaks it, and the fumes from other cars in heavy traffic can come in through the vent. Because you cannot sense it, prevention is the only defense. Remember: Carbon monoxide from the engine can kill and cannot be tasted, smelled or seen; it tends to leak while the heater runs, when the exhaust system is faulty, or from other cars' fumes in heavy traffic.

lines.text: No holding a device with any part of the body.
No writing, sending or reading texts.
No reaching out of position, no video.

narration.text: Under the Hands Free Tennessee law, a driver may not hold a phone or mobile device with any part of the body or write, send or read any text-based message. The law also forbids reaching for a device in a way that takes you out of your seated, belted position, and watching, recording or broadcasting video on it. So a phone balanced on your shoulder counts as holding it, and stretching to grab a phone from the floor is also forbidden. The device has to stay in hands-free mode, out of your hands. Remember: The hands-free law also forbids reaching for a device in a way that takes you out of your seated, belted position, and watching, recording or broadcasting video on it.

lines.text: Older rule: texting only.
Hands-free law: holding, texting, reaching, video.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Some drivers remember only the older rule and think that phone use is fine as long as they are not texting. The older two thousand nine rule bans reading or sending written messages on a hand-held device while moving, with a fine of up to fifty dollars plus up to ten dollars court costs, and exempts on-duty police, firefighters and emergency workers. The hands-free law goes much further: it bans holding the device at all, along with handling texts, reaching out of position and using video. Remember: Under the Hands Free Tennessee law, a driver may not hold a phone or mobile device with any part of the body or write, send or read any text-based message.

lines.text: Adults: hands-free only in flashing school zones.
Under eighteen: no exception.
No video screens in the driver's view.

narration.text: Since the start of two thousand eighteen, drivers aged eighteen or older commit an offense by using a hand-held phone while moving through a marked school zone with its warning flashers on, unless the phone is in hands-free mode. In a marked school zone, the hands-free exception does not cover drivers under eighteen, for whom hand-held use is a delinquent act. Separately, a video screen able to show television or video may not be installed where the driver can see it while the car is moving, though navigation, vehicle information and camera displays are allowed.

lines.text: What does the hands-free law forbid?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: what does the Hands Free Tennessee law forbid a driver to do with a phone or mobile device? Work it out before reading on. A driver may not hold the device with any part of the body, and may not write, send or read any text-based message. The law also forbids reaching for a device in a way that takes you out of your seated, belted position, and watching, recording or broadcasting video on it. That is far broader than the older rule, which covered only written messages. Remember: Under the Hands Free Tennessee law, a driver may not hold a phone or mobile device with any part of the body or write, send or read any text-based message.

lines.text: Carbon monoxide: prevent it.
Phones: hands off.
School zones: stricter for teens.

narration.text: To close, carbon monoxide can kill without any taste, smell or sight, so never run the engine in a closed garage or use the heater or air conditioner in a closed parked car, have the exhaust checked, listen for roaring and close the vent in heavy traffic. Under the hands-free law, do not hold a device, handle texts, reach out of position or use video. In a flashing school zone adults may use only hands-free mode, drivers under eighteen get no exception, and video screens must stay out of the driver's view. Remember: Never run the engine in a closed garage, and never use the heater or air conditioner in a parked car with the windows shut.
